This article puts the functions of **fastsae** in the order in which an analysis usually
goes, from the direct estimates of a survey to the tables that are published. The order is
a sensible default, not a theorem: each step says what it checks and what to do with the
answer. The example is the `mys` data (mean years of schooling of people with disabilities
in 42 regencies, 10 of them without a sample), so every output below comes from a real call.

| Step | Question | Functions |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | How good are the direct estimates? | `add_reliability_flags()`, `gvf_smooth()` |
| 2 | Is there spatial structure to model? | `create_weights()`, `spatial_test()` |
| 3 | Which covariates? | `step_sae()` |
| 4 | Which model? | `eblup_fh()`, `eblup_sfh()`, `compare_sae()` |
| 5 | Is the model adequate? | `diagnose()`, `autoplot()` |
| 6 | Do the estimates add up to a published total? | `benchmark_sae()` |
| 7 | How are the results reported? | `map_sae()`, `export_sae()` |

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(fastsae)
data("mys")
data("mys_proxmat")
```

## 1. Check the direct estimates

Small area models are worth fitting where the direct estimates are imprecise. Fit a first
model and flag each domain by the BPS reliability tiers (RSE up to 25%, 25-50%, above 50%):

```{r flags}
fit_full <- eblup_fh(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, vardir = ~vardir, data = mys, print_result = FALSE)
flags <- add_reliability_flags(fit_full)
table(flags$reliability)
```

The same tiers can be computed on the direct estimates alone, and this is what tells you
how much there is to gain. When `vardir` itself is noisy (small samples, so that the
estimated variances are themselves estimates), smooth it first with `gvf_smooth()`: a
Fay-Herriot model treats `vardir` as known, so noise in it goes straight into the
shrinkage. We use the `vardir` of `mys` as given here; see `?gvf_smooth` for the methods.

## 2. Is there spatial structure?

`spatial_test()` runs the tests before any spatial model is fitted: Moran's I on the
direct estimates and on the regression residuals, the Anselin LM tests, and a likelihood
ratio test of the Spatial Fay-Herriot model against the standard one. `create_weights()`
builds `W` from polygons or coordinates; `mys_proxmat` is ready-made here.

```{r spatial_test}
spatial_test(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, vardir = ~vardir, data = mys, W = mys_proxmat)
```

Read the tests together, not one at a time. Here the likelihood ratio test is just
significant, but the Moran's I of the residuals is negative and not significant, and the
spatial model puts the autocorrelation at the boundary:

```{r sfh_boundary}
fit_sfh_full <- eblup_sfh(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, vardir = ~vardir, data = mys,
                          W = mys_proxmat, print_result = FALSE)
fit_sfh_full$rho
```

A SAR parameter of $\rho = -1$ is on the edge of its parameter space (see the NEWS file
for how `eblup_sfh()` treats it), and it means negative, not positive, spatial
dependence, which is not the "neighbours resemble each other" pattern that motivates a
spatial model. On these data the evidence for a spatial effect is weak, and the
decision below is to keep the standard model. On data with clear positive clustering the
tests agree, and the spatial model is the choice.

## 3. Select the covariates

`step_sae()` searches the covariates by an information criterion (BIC by default) and
refits the model with the same settings at every step. For the EBLUP models it compares
fits by ML, because the REML likelihood cannot compare models with different covariates;
the selected model is then refitted with the method of the original.

```{r step}
sel <- step_sae(fit_full, trace = FALSE)
sel$path
formula(sel$model)
```

Select with the model you intend to use. With a spatial model, a spatially smooth
covariate and the spatial random effect explain the same variation, so the covariates kept
by a non-spatial search can be redundant once the spatial effect is in (see `?step_sae`).
Selection also optimises the criterion on the same data it is then fitted to, so the
standard errors of the selected model do not account for the search; treat the selected
model as a good description, not as a tested hypothesis.

## 4. Fit and compare the candidates

Fit the selected specification as a standard and as a spatial model and compare them on
the same domains:

```{r fit}
fit_fh <- eblup_fh(y ~ x2, vardir = ~vardir, data = mys, print_result = FALSE)
fit_sfh <- eblup_sfh(y ~ x2, vardir = ~vardir, data = mys, W = mys_proxmat,
                     print_result = FALSE)
compare_sae(fit_fh, fit_sfh, names = c("FH", "SFH"))
```

`compare_sae()` reports agreement (Bland-Altman limits, Lin's concordance correlation),
ranking, and efficiency. A model that is more efficient on paper is only better if it is
also right: the MSE ratio is computed under each model's own assumptions, so a smaller MSE
does not by itself justify a model whose spatial parameter sits on the boundary. Here the
two sets of estimates are very close, and the simpler model is kept.

When the response is a proportion, a count or a skewed positive quantity, or you want the
uncertainty as a posterior, use `hb_area()` instead (see the
[Bayesian article](hb-area-inla.html)); with unit-level data, `eblup_bhf()` or `hb_unit()`
(see the [unit-level article](unit-level-bhf.html)). `step_sae()` and `compare_sae()` work
with those too. If the MSE matters more than the point estimates, `eblup_sfh()` and
`eblup_stfh()` also have a parametric bootstrap MSE (`mse_type = "pbmse"`), run in parallel.

## 5. Check the model

```{r diagnose}
diag_fh <- diagnose(fit_fh, W = mys_proxmat[!is.na(mys$y), !is.na(mys$y)])
diag_fh$precision[c("mean_direct_rse", "mean_sae_rse", "prop_reliable")]
diag_fh$goodness_of_fit[c("w_stat", "df", "p_value")]
```

`diagnose()` reports the gain in precision against the direct estimates, the goodness of
fit of Brown et al. (2001), the descriptive calibration regression, and the residual
spatial autocorrelation; see the [diagnostics article](model-diagnostics.html) for how
to read each. The plots are one call away:

```{r diag_plot}
autoplot(diag_fh, type = "calibration")
```

Two things to look for: a calibration slope far from 1 together with a visible pattern in
the residuals, which means a missing covariate or a wrong link; and residuals that are
spatially clustered, which is the cue to go back to step 2.

## 6. Benchmark to a published total

Official statistics often have to add up: the area estimates must reproduce a
published estimate for the whole population. `benchmark_sae()` adjusts a fitted model after
the fact. The target must come from outside the model, such as the national direct estimate
of the same survey. Here the sample-weighted mean of the direct estimates stands in for it:

```{r benchmark}
national <- weighted.mean(mys$y, mys$weight, na.rm = TRUE)
bm <- benchmark_sae(fit_fh, target = national, weight = mys$weight, method = "ratio")

c(target = national,
  before = weighted.mean(bm$original, mys$weight),
  after = weighted.mean(bm$benchmarked, mys$weight))
```

The weights should be the population shares of the domains. `mys$weight` is a *sample*
share, used here only so that the example runs. With sample shares, the benchmark
reproduces a figure that is not the population mean. The ratio, difference, optimal and
logit methods differ in how they spread the adjustment and in what happens to the MSE (see
`?benchmark_sae`); benchmarking also adds to the MSE of the adjusted estimates (the `mse_benchmarked`
column of the result). If you want the constraint built into the fit, use
`self_benchmark = TRUE` in the model function instead.

## 7. Report

`map_sae()` draws choropleth maps of the estimate, its RSE or its reliability tier from an
`sf` object, and `export_sae()` writes the estimates, the reliability flags and the
benchmarked values to a spreadsheet:

```{r export, eval = requireNamespace("writexl", quietly = TRUE) || requireNamespace("openxlsx", quietly = TRUE)}
out <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
invisible(export_sae(fit_fh, file = out, benchmark = bm))
file.exists(out)
```

```{r map, eval = FALSE}
# needs polygons: an sf object with one row per domain and a key to match `domain`
map_sae(fit_fh, sf_geom = polygons, key = "area_id", type = "estimate")
map_sae(fit_fh, sf_geom = polygons, key = "area_id", type = "reliability")
```

Report the RSE or the reliability tier next to every estimate, and say which areas have no
direct estimate (`mys$area[is.na(mys$y)]`): their value comes from the model alone.

## Summary of the decisions

1. Start from the reliability of the direct estimates; fit a model where it pays.
2. Test for spatial structure, and require the tests and the estimated parameter to agree
   before adding a spatial effect.
3. Select covariates with the model you will use.
4. Compare candidates on agreement and on the adequacy checks, not on the MSE alone.
5. Check calibration, residuals and residual spatial autocorrelation before publishing.
6. Benchmark only to a target from outside the model, with population weights.
7. Publish the uncertainty and the reliability tier with every estimate.

## References

- Brown, G., Chambers, R., Heady, P., & Heasman, D. (2001). Evaluation of small area estimation methods: An application to unemployment estimates from the UK LFS. *Proceedings of Statistics Canada Symposium 2001: Achieving Data Quality in a Statistical Agency*.
- Rao, J. N. K., & Molina, I. (2015). *Small Area Estimation* (2nd ed.). John Wiley & Sons.
